status_summary: Public Law 119-21 (signed 2025-07-04) section 71119 requires states to establish Medicaid community engagement requirements for certain adults, going beyond the Mandate's call for state options by making the requirement mandatory. CMS published an interim final rule on 2026-06-03 (effective 2026-07-31; correction 2026-06-29): adults in the expansion group must show 80 hours a month of work, community service, a work program or education, or equivalent income, subject to exclusions and verification, with state compliance required by 2027-01-01. Twenty-three States, the District of Columbia and the Governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania sued on 2026-06-29 (Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. Oz, D. Mass.); on 2026-07-29 Judge Richard G. Stearns denied a preliminary injunction without prejudice for lack of irreparable harm, and on 2026-10-29 he vacated the part of the rule's medically frail definition requiring a condition to significantly impair the ability to comply and enjoined applying it to the plaintiff States, upholding the twelve-month lookback and self-attestation limit and leaving the rest of the rule and the 2027-01-01 date in place. The same law adds six-month eligibility renewals for the expansion adult group (section 71107, for renewals on or after 2027-01-01, with CMS guidance in a 2026-03-06 State Medicaid Director Letter) and cost sharing for certain expansion adults (section 71120, effective 2028-10-01 per CMS); no time limit or lifetime cap on benefits appears in the CMS summaries of the law.

timeline.event: Public Law 119-21 is signed; Title VII, Subtitle B, Chapter 1 includes sections 71107 (eligibility redeterminations), 71119 (community engagement requirement) and 71120 (cost sharing for expansion adults).
CMS issues State Medicaid Director Letter #26-001 on implementing six-month eligibility renewals for the adult expansion group under section 71107, for renewals scheduled on or after 2027-01-01.
CMS publishes the interim final rule implementing the community engagement requirement (CMS-2454-IFC, 91 FR 33348).
Federal Register publishes a correction to the interim final rule.

A coalition of 24 attorneys general (23 states and the District of Columbia) and the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania sues over the CMS interim final rule (Massachusetts et al. v. Oz), alleging it unlawfully narrows the medically frail exemption, violates the Administrative Procedure Act and coerces states.

Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) issued a Memorandum and Order on Plaintiffs' Motion for a Preliminary Injunction (Document 94) in Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. Oz (No. 1:26-cv-12962-RGS), denying the States' motion without prejudice because they had not shown irreparable harm, noting the Government's representation that it would reimburse 90 percent of state eligibility-system costs and observing that the tight timeline was set by Congress in H.R. 1, not by the interim final rule; the court stated that the decision reflected no view on the merits and that it would set an expedited schedule for full merits briefing before the 2027-01-01 implementation deadline.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Document 94 (RECAP copy of the filed order)

timeline.event: Interim final rule takes effect; the comment period closes the same day.

In Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. Oz (D. Mass. No. 1:26-cv-12962-RGS), Judge Richard G. Stearns heard argument on the plaintiffs' Motion for Partial Summary Judgment (Doc. 103, filed 2026-09-01) and the defendants' Cross Motion for Summary Judgment (Doc. 138, filed 2026-09-18) and took the matter under advisement (docket entry 145).

Judge Richard G. Stearns, in a Memorandum and Order on Cross-Motions for Summary Judgment in Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. Oz (D. Mass. No. 1:26-cv-12962-RGS, Document 147), allows in part and denies in part both motions: the interim final rule's added condition that a medically frail individual's condition significantly impair the ability to comply with the community engagement requirement is held beyond CMS's authority and contrary to law, while the twelve-month lookback for claims and encounter data and the limit on self-attestation are held not arbitrary or capricious, and the Spending Clause claim is not reached. An Order of Vacatur and Enjoinment (Document 148) vacates that portion of the rule under 5 U.S.C. 706(2), enjoins applying it to the plaintiff States and bars penalizing them for errors or delays in implementing the rule for six months; the Judgment (Document 149) enters judgment for the plaintiffs on Count I and partial judgment for the defendants on Count II and dismisses the case. The court states that the six-month stay of enforcement does not affect the statutory 2027-01-01 implementation date.

title: Add Medicaid work requirements, cost sharing and stronger eligibility checks
uncertainties: The interim final rule was read on the Federal Register host for its first 100,000 of about 131,000 characters; the good-faith exemption section was not reached there, and the latest exemption end date of 2028-12-31 comes from a CMS overview deck. Sections 71107 and 71120 were confirmed through CMS documents on the medicaid.gov host (State Medicaid Director Letter #26-001 and the November 2025 legislation overview slide), not the statute body, which the GovInfo page truncates. The 2026-07-29 order (Document 94) was read on 2026-10-28 in a RECAP copy of the filed order, with the docket on CourtListener (last updated 2026-10-27). The order lists 23 States, the District of Columbia and the Governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania as plaintiffs, which matches the California release (24 attorneys general and two governors); the figure of 25 states in trade press matches that list only if the two Governors' states are counted. The order decided only the preliminary injunction motion and stated that it did not anticipate the court's views on the merits; the cross-motions for summary judgment were decided on 2026-10-29 (Documents 147 to 149); whether the government will appeal, and how CMS will apply the medically frail definition after the vacatur in non-plaintiff states, is not known as of 2026-10-30. Early implementation by individual states and Section 1115 work requirement waivers were not reviewed.
